name: Chitosan (supplements by mouth)
short: Case reports: anaphylaxis (hives, breathing difficulty) after oral chitosan; INR rose in a man on warfarin, again on restart. Review caution: crustacean allergy. Trials: mostly mild events.
text: Allergy: a case report describes a 47-year-old woman who developed hives over her whole body and difficulty breathing after taking a chitosan-containing health food by mouth, with positive skin tests to chitosan; the authors diagnosed an immediate-type allergy and say they knew of no earlier report of such a reaction, though contact dermatitis from chitosan-containing creams had been reported. That abstract describes chitosan as existing in the cell walls of zygomycetes and does not mention shellfish. A review notes that chitosan is made from chitin, found especially in crustaceans, and says it cannot be recommended to people allergic to crustaceans; this is a caution, not an observed reaction. In a challenge study of a chitosan bandage applied to the skin (a different route), none of the 10 people with shellfish allergy who completed it had a reaction or a positive skin test to chitosan powder. A case report is titled as anaphylaxis after chitosan was injected into a joint (a different route); its abstract gives no details of the case, saying that allergic reactions to chitosan have been reported on rare occasions and that the authors report a case of allergy. A letter with no abstract is titled 'Safety of chitosan processed wine in shrimp allergic patients'; its title gives no results. Blood thinners: a case report describes a marked rise in the INR in an 83-year-old man on warfarin after he started chitosan, which recurred when he took it again; the authors rated chitosan the probable cause and suggest it reduced vitamin K absorption. A 2021 systematic review of food and supplement interactions with warfarin names chitosan among products for which healthcare professionals should be aware of an increased risk of bleeding. Trials: a Cochrane review of 15 randomised trials (1,219 overweight or obese adults) found no clear differences between chitosan and control groups in the frequency of adverse events, while noting that many trials were of poor quality. In a 105-patient trial in high cholesterol with four chitosan doses and a placebo group, 24 patients (23%) reported 29 mostly mild treatment-related adverse events, most often constipation and diarrhoea (3.0% each); the abstract does not split these by group. The review that gives the crustacean caution reports mild, transient nausea and constipation in 2.6 to 5.4% of subjects, and no clinically significant symptoms compared with placebo in trials of up to 12 weeks. In an 8-week trial in 65 adults, blood levels of vitamins A, E and D and of carotenes did not differ between groups.
